newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: UN protests after Tajik troops beat up observers.
newsitem.headline: UN protests after Tajik troops beat up observers.

text.p: Two United Nations military observers and their local translator were beaten, robbed and lined up for a mock execution by Tajik government soldiers, the U.N. observer mission in the capital Dushanbe said on Wednesday.

The mission, known as UNMOT, has protested to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, whose Moscow-backed troops have been fighting Islamist guerrillas for nearly five years in the mountainous former Soviet state bordering China and Afghanistan.

It said in a statement that UNMOT was "gravely concerned" about the "use of force, physical assault and threat against the lives of UNMOT military observers and a civilian staff member by government servicemen in Chorsade on December 3".

Hans Schalk, an Austrian army captain, Imran Shavkat, a Bangladeshi lieutenant, and a Tajik translator were stopped on Tuesday by government soldiers in Chorsade, about 140 km (90 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe. The soldiers demanded they escort them to territory held by rebel forces.

When the observers refused, the statement said, "UNMOT team members were physically assaulted with weapons, kicked and punched by government servicemen and lined up in a row to be shot...There were also attempts to push one of the UNMOT team members off a mountain edge."

The officers, after having their communications equipment confiscated, were then told to drive to rebel-held territory and bring back government troops allegedly held hostage. The U.N. officers were told that if they failed they would be shot.
As they drove off, their vehicle came under heavy artillery and small arms fire as they headed for rebel-held territory.
They were later helped by Islamist guerrillas to reach a U.N. observer post in Garm, 200 km (130 miles) east of Dushanbe, the site of heavy fighting over the weekend.
The whole U.N. team was subsequently ordered out of Garm by the United Nations on Wednesday. They drove north to the border with Kyrgyzstan.

The beating may reinforce many diplomats' belief that the United Nations observers in Tajikistan, first deployed in 1994, have no real role left to play in the civil war that has raged since the break-up of the Soviet Union.
A U.N.-sponsored ceasefire collapsed shortly after it was reconfirmed last July.
The announcement last week of peace talks between Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri in northern Afghanistan on December 9 was followed by a flare-up in fighting round Garm.
The rebels appeared to be advancing slowly but surely towards the capital.
Tens of thousands have died in the war and made many more have been made homeless.
